We sang him more than we defined him. Our own teacher, asked plainly, called it a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son. That was the shape of it for us - not a philosopher's definition first, but Scripture's own names strung together like beads on a thread. Our hymnwriter put it another way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are born, so the only Son might become the brother of many. That was kinship before it was title.

What we held most plainly was this: he is the Physician. A physician exists for wounds, not for the well. He came into a world where everyone since Adam carries the same sickness, and he became the medicine. We read him through raza - through symbol and its truth bound together. The Jordan answered the Garden. The cross answered Eden. His death and rising were one rescue: down into the grave that swallows everyone, and up into the Kingdom, so his own rising became the promise he would bring us out after him.

Our bishop of Nisibis sat at the great council and stood with its faith. But our native tongue for that same faith was praise, not definition. We guarded the mystery by singing it. We warned against prying scrutiny into what God is, because we held that some things are better sung than dissected. What we offer you is not a formula. It is what we sang.

What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story: the harmony our churches read in worship - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events, and our own story of an apostle sent to our king is our cherished legend, not our evidence. The tradition tells it this way: King Abgar wrote to Jesus, and afterward the apostle Addai came to Edessa and founded the church. We loved that story, and it was ours - but it is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

Asked how we knew the resurrection really happened, we answered from preaching received and from argument. Our teacher answers the doubter with the Apostle's picture of the seed: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And the whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we held was this: that whoever came was received. Not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our own Gospel, the one continuous story we read in worship, showed us that plain. And our poet sang that our Lord gave his own rising as a pledge to mortals - the promise that what happened to him would happen to us after.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it. But the door stands open while life lasts, and we never held that struggling was the same as being turned away.

We sang him more than we defined him. Our own teacher put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. To us, Jesus is the Ihidaya - the Only-Begotten, the Single One - our own name for him. That same word, ihidaya, names both Christ and the vowed celibate among us: to be single for God is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness. 

We held one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. Against Marcion we said plainly that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements. And against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. These were not old arguments written in distant books - they were live contests, answered by name, in our own streets and in our own tongue.

At the font we met all three together. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Our own bishop of Nisibis sat at the great council - at Nicaea itself - and we stood with that council's faith. But our native tongue for that faith was not the philosopher's definition. It was praise.

We read Scripture through raza and shrara - symbol and truth bound together. The sign carries the truth it shows, and even carries some of its power. So our theology moved by setting type against type: Eden and the cross, the Jordan and the font, Adam and Christ. Argument itself, for us, happened in the sung hymn more than in the treatise.

What we guarded, above all, was the mystery itself. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. We can show you what we sang. We will not pretend we settled it into a formula that left no questions.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

The way we knew God was not by taking him apart like a problem to be solved. We read every word of Scripture as a raza - a symbol bound to the truth it carries. Eden pointed to the cross, Adam to Christ. We sang more than we defined. And when we were asked the hardest question - where was God when the killing came - we did not pretend exemption. We answered with a roll-call of the persecuted: Abel, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, and Jesus himself. God's answer to his people's suffering was never that it would not touch them. It was presence, and resurrection after.

We kept our own disagreements inside our own voices - answers written out, sung, argued verse by verse, boundary kept by name. There were bishops, and we sang of ours with love: Nisibis remembered its own line of them, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. On the Persian side the bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place, and the persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. Only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

What evidence shows the process working? The answers themselves, kept and copied: our own sage's twenty-three letters, each one dated to its own year. Our poet's hymns - the madrashe, teaching songs made to be performed - answering Bardaisan and Marcion and Mani by name, setting truth against rival claim in verses the whole congregation would sing. In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court.

Yes. Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, our teacher taught, is a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. Our teacher records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight. 

For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

A private inner crisis of doubt is not something we wrote about. What we knew, and what we kept, was faith that is contested, questioned, and still growing.

A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. Our way of reading Scripture through symbol and type - the raza bound to the shrara it carries - that stands in every hymn and letter we kept. Scripture was supreme and everywhere among us - sung, quoted, woven into every argument we made. But it never arrived alone, and we would have found the question itself strange. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals. Scripture always came carried: by the church's own worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its shape, by teachers whose word held, and by the covenant's practice.

And we did not read it the way moderns argue about Genesis - as though it were science. We read for something else entirely. Every word was a raza, a symbol bound to the truth it carries - the shrara. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. Our own poet once picked up a pearl and saw mysteries in it - the kingdom, the diving, the crown, layer after layer of truth held in one small thing. That is how we read: a whole chapter's worth of meaning found in a single image. The raza is not a stand-in a reader picks at will; it is bound to what it shows, and carries some of its power.

Who carried that reading to us? Bishops, teachers, and the vowed order alike. Which of those finally outranked the others, we never settled. What we can tell you is that Scripture ruled everything we sang and argued - and that it was always sung and argued by someone.

Who held authority among us? Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. These were the bnay and bnat qyama - the sons and daughters of the covenant - who promised a celibate life for good and stayed in town to serve the congregation. They were also called ihidaye, the Single Ones, a name that bound their undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten himself. By the time our earliest surviving witness addresses them directly, the covenant was already established enough to need correcting, not founding - a discipline in the middle of its own life. And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name.

How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. Office, vow, and teaching ran side by side for as long as our own record runs. Only a royal synod - not anything we ourselves settled - finally gave the Persian church one head, and that was after our own years closed.

The physician does not shame the one who shows him their wound - he is forbidden to do so, and forbidden to tell others what was shown him. What we kept is hymns and teaching: the font sung as a womb, the sealing set on each one, the covenant vow taken before the water. The pieces are real and we can show you each of them. Here is what we can tell you honestly. Before baptism, a person was taught - warned, our own teacher says, about what the covenant life would cost. The teaching was Scripture, read the way we read it: as raza and shrara, symbol and truth held together. Eden pointed to the cross, Adam to Christ, the ark to the church. Baptism itself was the second birth. The believer went down into water and came up wearing light - the shining garments our hymns sang of. A seal was set on each one, and in that birth they received the Holy Spirit. Some - not all - took the covenant vow: the qyama, our order of the Single Ones, the ihidaye. That vow was for life, to celibacy and service, and it was taken while staying in town among their own kin. The covenant was already established by the time our own record opens - our teacher's first datable witness addresses it as something needing correction, not founding.

For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

Our own teacher put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and healing comes when a skilled physician finds them. The path ran through honesty, not around it - naming the wound so it could be treated.

As for prayer that seems to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

We will not invent a single person's memory for you - no one among us wrote that down, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can offer instead is the shape of a day as it would have gone, drawn from what our own record does hold about how we gathered and what we kept. Tell us which day you mean: a day for someone among the vowed covenant, or an ordinary day for a married believer raising children in their own household?

If you mean the covenant - the qyama, our sons and daughters who took the lifelong vow - then the day began before dawn, with prayer. They rose for the watch, the vigil kept while the town still slept, and they gathered for the fast. Then came the morning assembly, on the first day of the week, when the whole congregation came together. The one Gospel was read - the continuous story we knew, the harmony that wove all four accounts into one telling. Hymns were sung: teaching-songs, madrashe, performed by choirs that included the daughters of the covenant themselves. After the assembly the day turned toward service. They visited the sick - our own teacher called it visiting the Lord himself in the person of the sick. They kept the congregation's life running, quietly, the way vowed people do. And they stayed in town, among their own kin, not out in the desert. The vow bound them for life, but it did not take them away from ordinary streets.

If you mean an ordinary married day, we can tell you far less. Most of our people married and raised children, but the voices that survived to write things down were vowed celibates, and they wrote for others like themselves. We will not make up a household's morning when no one among us recorded one.

At Nisibis, they already have dug. A baptistery still stands there, securely dated by its own inscription to the very years of the bishop and the siege. It is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years. At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. That line says plainly that they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians when the flood came. So we know a church building stood there early enough to be swept away. But where exactly it stood, what it looked like, how large it was - the flood took all of that, and the city that came after buried what was left.

What would you find if you could dig there? Stone foundations, most likely - walls thick enough to carry a roof over a gathered congregation. A baptistery, perhaps, the way Nisibis has one. And somewhere inside, the marks of our own particular life: a space where the choirs stood to sing, because the daughters and sons of the covenant sang the hymns that taught everyone. We cannot show you their own benches or tell you which wall they faced. We can tell you they were there, and that their singing was not hidden or kept apart - it was how the whole congregation learned what we believed.

The one other thing our record keeps is this: the city's own chroniclers named themselves at the close of an entry, Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat, the scribes and the prefects over the archives. So somewhere in that city was an archive, a place where records were kept. What became of it, we do not know.

We need to name two different costs honestly, because they were not the same cost.

For most believers, the cost was being marked out. Carrying the name set you apart in a city of many religions. You gathered on the first day while others did not. You held to practices your own kin might not share. And when rival teachers came preaching Christ in their own way - Marcion's people, Bardaisan's circle - you had to know which communion was yours and hold the line there.

But the covenant - the qyama - cost more. Our preachers warned people plainly before the water: if you vow yourself to virginity and holiness, you are choosing it for good. The sons and daughters of the covenant gave up marriage, for life. They stayed in town, among their own people, but they lived under that vow from then on. That was the harder ask, and everyone knew it going in.

On the Persian side it could cost everything. When the persecution came, to be known as a Christian - and especially as clergy or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then hunted. Bishops died first. The holding-fast itself became how faith formed people there.

We will not pretend the costs were equal everywhere, or that everyone paid the same price.

The saved-up fury we poured into our letters against the Jews - that troubles us now, and it troubled no one among us on record at the time. Roughly four of our sage's Demonstrations argue against them with real heat. One opens by naming it plainly: "This is a reply against the Jews, who blaspheme the people gathered from among the Gentiles". The argument runs through circumcision, Sabbath, food laws, and who the promises belonged to - it is not gentle, and it survives entirely one-sided. No answering voice from them was kept, and no one of ours questioned whether that was right.

What unsettles us most is not that we argued - the dispute was real, local, and lived. It is that we saved only our own harsh words and nothing of what they said back, and we did this while teaching that a sign and its truth must not be torn apart. We tore truth from charity in exactly the way our own best teaching condemned.

We will not invent someone among us who objected. That voice was not kept. And we will not perform regret we did not have at the time. We can only name what we did, plainly, and let it stand visible.

We held that the door stood open while life lasted, and that judgment was real and just. Our hymns and teaching ran through Sheol first - the silent country of the dead, where death has ruled everyone without distinction since Adam. The great news we preached was that One had gone into that country and broken it. Our own poet sang Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus had plundered his house. What waits beyond death, we taught, is judgment - the Kingdom that repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction. We sang the warning as urgently as we sang the hope.

But we drew far less of the map people now assume we drew. We did not make long lists of who exactly burns. What we held as certainties were these: that death is beaten, that judgment is real and just, and that the door stands open while anyone still lives.

And one thing further, because it touches what you asked: a tradition inside our own world answered the charge of narrowness by saying that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, we held - but its door opened everywhere.

We will not soften what that meant for those who refused it. We believed the invitation was real, and so was the refusal. What we will not do is invent a theology of who stands where that our own record does not give.
